progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: bio-m8-b02 (endotherms make most of their heat by metabolism and regulate core temperature by negative feedback; heat flows from hotter to cooler; vasodilation, sweating, shivering; physiological, behavioural and structural adaptations; trends: compact, insulated bodies in cold climates, large extremities in hot ones; "thick fur or blubber, which slows heat loss"; feedback has limits), bio-m8-b01 (the five-part loop), Year 11 practical skills and the Module 7 practicals bio-m7-p02 and bio-m7-p05 (aim, independent, dependent and controlled variables, a control, repeats, a risk table as a format). Not assumed: the word "model" in its scientific sense, cooling curves, surface area to volume ratio as a number (b02 named the trend only), the VRA words as s07 defines them (s07 comes after p02 in the Biology playlist; this video uses its three plain questions without the target picture, as p02 does). Start: a safe model method: two flasks of warm water, one wrapped in cotton wool. Stop: graph the cooling data, read rates from it, and evaluate the control variables and the model's limits. Next handoff: bio-m8-b03, "How do insulin and glucagon regulate glucose?" (route next).
progression.startsWith: Fur and blubber slow heat loss. Testing it on live animals isn't practical, or kind. But you can wrap a flask of warm water and leave another bare. After twenty minutes, the bare flask has cooled about twice as much. So how do you run this fairly, and what can a flask really tell you about an animal?
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why a model is used and how a wrapped flask maps onto fur and a body; stating the aim and variables for an insulation comparison; naming the bare flask as the control; setting up with equal volumes, the same starting temperature, the same lids and position; explaining why the starting temperature must be the same (bigger difference, faster heat loss); recording readings in a table with units in the headings; drawing a cooling-curve graph (axes, units, points, smooth curves, key); calculating an average cooling rate (drop ÷ time) and a mean; explaining why the curves flatten; judging the spread against the gap; concluding narrowly with the still-air reason; naming what the model can't show (no metabolic heat, no feedback, fur can be raised or wet); judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing a three-row risk assessment; calculating and explaining a surface area to volume comparison; identifying and fixing two uncontrolled variables.
progression.nextLesson: how insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose in range (bio-m8-b03).

teaching.task: Fur slows heat loss. How do you test that fairly without an animal, and what can the test really tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the claim and why a model (no animal or person); (2) how fur insulates (still air) and how the model maps onto it; (3) aim and variables; (4) set-up, control and lids; (5) prediction: why the same start matters; (6) readings in a table; (7) graphing; (8) reading rates from the graph, and why the curves flatten; (9) repeats, means, spread against gap, conclusion and its reason; (10) what the model can't show; (11) VRA; (12) risk; attempts; decision rule and handoff; key notes.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Fur and blubber slow heat loss. Recall that heat flows from a warmer body to cooler air. The aim: find out how an insulating layer affects the rate of heat loss from a model body. The bare flask is the control, the comparison without insulation. Here's a quick prediction. Record each temperature every four minutes for twenty minutes. Graph temperature against time, with a curve for each insulation condition. A steeper line means faster cooling. Run three trials in total, starting from forty five each time. Now be careful what you claim. Now judge it with three questions. The risk assessment. Your turn. Nine divided by ten is point nine degrees per minute for the small beaker, and three divided by ten is point three for the large. One more. One: the starting temperatures differed. So for this insulation test: change only the wrap, keep the volume and starting temperature the same, repeat each trial, graph it, and claim only what the model can show.
teaching.openingDecision: Fur and blubber slow heat loss. Testing it on live animals isn't practical, or kind. But you can wrap a flask of warm water and leave another bare. After twenty minutes, the bare flask has cooled about twice as much. So how do you run this fairly, and what can a flask really tell you about an animal?
teaching.understandingCheck: a 2 s prediction (5, not a practice question); two unseen HSC-style items with every condition visible (A1: same shape, both volumes, the same start, the same room, both drops, the time, two demands; A2: both volumes and temperatures, the wrapping, the result, the claim, the demand). 10 seconds each with the invitation to pause; nothing answer-bearing. One crossed mistake each.
